title: Is Agentic Code Review Helpful? Mining Developers' Feedback to CodeRabbit Reviews in the Wild
hook: CodeRabbit leaves review comments on hundreds of thousands of real pull requests. A large-scale study of how developers actually respond finds more than half get rejected outright.
key_points: Mined 31,073 review-comment/developer-feedback pairs from 10,191 pull requests across 239 GitHub repositories.
Only 36.4% of comments were accepted, 7.3% sparked discussion, and 56.3% were rejected outright.
Rejections mostly trace to invalid suggestions (false positives, redundant, out of scope) or misalignment with dev intent.
Reviews skew toward functional concerns over evolvability (maintainability/design) ones, yet are more often wrong on the latter.
A lightweight learned classifier predicts whether a review will be rejected with up to 76% F1.
content_html: CodeRabbit leaves automated review comments on hundreds of thousands of real pull requests. A large-scale study of how developers actually respond finds more than half get rejected outright.
extra_html:
What they measured

The authors mined 31,073 review-comment/developer-feedback pairs from 10,191 pull requests across 239 GitHub repositories. Only 36.4% of CodeRabbit's comments were accepted, 7.3% sparked further discussion, and 56.3% were rejected, mostly because the suggestion was invalid (a false positive, redundant, or out of scope) or misaligned with what the developer actually intended or how the project usually does things. The reviews also skewed toward functional correctness over longer-term evolvability concerns like maintainability and design, yet were more often wrong specifically on the evolvability side.

Why it matters

The authors trained lightweight learning-based classifiers to predict, from the comment and its context, whether a review would be rejected, reaching up to 76% F1 — meaning rejection isn't random noise; there are learnable patterns in when agentic review comments miss the mark. That's a concrete lever: teams, or the tool itself, could use such a predictor to suppress low-value comments before they ever reach a developer. Lin, Liang, and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Govern the Repository, Not the Agent
related.hook: Across 930,000+ agent-authored pull requests, half the friction of merging code traces to the repository, not the agent — and AI contributions concentrate that risk 2x more than human ones.

related.title: Anchored Self-Play for Code Repair
related.hook: Let a model train itself by writing bugs and fixing them, and you get a free difficulty curriculum — until it invents bugs no real codebase would produce. Anchored Self-Play keeps it honest.

flashcards.prompt: What fraction of CodeRabbit's automated review comments were accepted vs. rejected, per this study?
flashcards.back_html: 36.4% were accepted (7.3% sparked discussion) while 56.3% were rejected outright, across 31,073 review/feedback pairs from 239 repos.

flashcards.prompt: Why were most CodeRabbit comments rejected?

choices.text: They were invalid (false positives, redundant, out of scope) or misaligned with developer intent and project conventions
Developers rejected almost all comments regardless of content, out of principle
CodeRabbit only ever commented on trivial whitespace issues

flashcards.explanation_html: Rejections traced mainly to invalid suggestions and misalignment with what the developer actually wanted or how the codebase normally works.

flashcards.prompt: What did the study find about functional vs. evolvability-focused review comments?
flashcards.back_html: Comments skewed toward functional concerns over evolvability (maintainability/design) concerns, yet were more often wrong specifically on the evolvability side.

flashcards.prompt: What's significant about the classifier reaching 76% F1 at predicting review rejection?

choices.text: It shows rejection isn't random — a lightweight model can learn patterns in which review comments developers will reject
It proves CodeRabbit's suggestions are correct 76% of the time
It means 76% of all pull requests in the study got rejected

flashcards.explanation_html: The F1 score belongs to a separate classifier predicting rejection, not to CodeRabbit's own suggestion accuracy — it shows learnable structure in what makes developers reject a comment.
